prompt: Which answer completes the addition tree shown in the picture?

solutions.title: Add level by level
solutions.body:
- Left box: $2 + 0 = 2$
- Right box: $1 + 3 = 4$
- Bottom box: $2 + 4 = 6$

**Answer: (E) 6**

solutions.title: Add everything at once
solutions.body:
Every number at the top ends up in the bottom box exactly once, so the answer is just $2 + 0 + 1 + 3 = 6$.

**Answer: (E) 6**

prompt: Nathalie wanted to build a large cube out of lots of small cubes. How many cubes are missing from the picture on the right that would be needed to build the large cube on the left?

solutions.title: Count the cubes that are there
solutions.body:
The large cube is $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ small cubes.

In the right picture, write the height of each stack on a $3 \times 3$ map (back row on top, front corner at the bottom):

| 3 | 3 | 3 |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | 3 |
| 1 | 1 | 2 |

Cubes present: $9 + 7 + 4 = 20$. Missing: $27 - 20 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

solutions.title: Count the gaps directly
solutions.body:
Compare each stack with a full stack of 3:

- Back row: 3, 3, 3 → nothing missing.
- Middle row: 2, 2, 3 → $1 + 1 + 0 = 2$ missing.
- Front row: 1, 1, 2 → $2 + 2 + 1 = 5$ missing.

Total missing: $2 + 5 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

prompt: How far must Maria walk to reach her friend Bianca?

solutions.title: Use the first eighth
solutions.body:
The 100 m mark shows the distance from Maria to the $\frac{1}{8}$ mark. So $\frac{1}{8}$ of the way is 100 m, and the whole way is $8 \times 100 = 800$ m.

**Answer: (C) 800 m**

solutions.title: Double up
solutions.body:
- $\frac{1}{8}$ of the way = 100 m
- $\frac{1}{4}$ = 200 m
- $\frac{1}{2}$ = 400 m
- whole way = 800 m

**Answer: (C) 800 m**

prompt: Nick can turn right but not left on his bicycle. What is the least number of right turns he must make in order to get from A to B?

solutions.title: Follow the only possible route
solutions.body:
Nick starts at A riding up (north). B is up and to the **left**, but he may not turn left.

- He rides up until the street ends at the long block and must turn **right** (1).
- At the right edge he turns right to go down (2).
- At the bottom he turns right to go left (3).
- At the left edge he turns right to go up (4) and rides straight to B.

**Answer: (B) 4**

solutions.title: Why fewer is impossible
solutions.body:
His first turn is forced: at the end of his street he must turn right, which takes him **away** from B. To head left again he needs two more right turns (first down, then left) — and now he is on the bottom street, below B. One more right turn is needed to ride up to B. That makes at least 4, and the route above uses exactly 4.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: Anna, Bob and Chris are altogether 31 years old. How old will all three be altogether in three years' time?

solutions.title: Each person gets older
solutions.body:
In 3 years each of the 3 children is 3 years older, so the total grows by $3 \times 3 = 9$.

$31 + 9 = 40$.

**Answer: (E) 40**

solutions.title: Try example ages
solutions.body:
Pick ages that add to 31, e.g. 10, 10 and 11. In 3 years: 13, 13 and 14, which add to 40.

**Answer: (E) 40**

prompt: In the following sum the same digit is used in each square: $\square\square \times \square = 176$. Which digit must be used so that the sum is correct?

solutions.title: Look at the last digit
solutions.body:
The last digit of $\square \times \square$ must be 6. Squares ending in 6: $4 \times 4 = 16$ and $6 \times 6 = 36$.

- $44 \times 4 = 176$ ✓
- $66 \times 6 = 396$ ✗

**Answer: (B) 4**

solutions.title: Estimate
solutions.body:
A two-digit number with equal digits times the same digit: $11 \times d \times d$. We need $11 \times d \times d = 176$, so $d \times d = 16$ and $d = 4$.

**Answer: (B) 4**

prompt: Michael must take a tablet every 15 minutes. He takes the first at 11:05. When does he take the fourth?

solutions.title: Count the gaps
solutions.body:
Between the 1st and 4th tablets there are only **3** gaps of 15 minutes: 45 minutes. $11:05 + 45$ min $= 11:50$.

**Answer: (B) 11:50**

prompt: Anne has a few grey tiles like the one in the picture. What is the maximum number of these tiles that she can place on the 5 × 4 rectangle without any overlaps?

solutions.title: Find a good arrangement
solutions.body:
Each tile covers 4 squares and the rectangle has 20, so at most 5 could fit. Four tiles fit (rows 1–4 from the top, columns 1–5 from the left):

- Tile 1: column 1, rows 1–3, plus row 2 column 2
- Tile 2: row 1, columns 2–4, plus row 2 column 3
- Tile 3: column 5, rows 1–3, plus row 2 column 4
- Tile 4: row 4, columns 2–4, plus row 3 column 3

Five tiles would have to cover every square with no gaps — the second method shows that can't happen.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Chessboard colouring
solutions.body:
Colour the rectangle like a chessboard: 10 black and 10 white squares.

Wherever you put a T-tile, it covers 3 squares of one colour and 1 of the other. With 5 tiles the counts can't both be 10: each tile makes the difference between black and white change by 2, and five changes of 2 (each either plus or minus) can never add up to 0.

So 5 tiles is impossible, and 4 tiles can be placed.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: The number 36 has the following property: 36 can be divided by its units digit without a remainder (36 is divisible by 6). With the number 38 this doesn't work. How many numbers between 20 and 30 have the same property as 36?

solutions.title: Think about the tens
solutions.body:
A number $2d$ is $20 + d$. It is divisible by $d$ exactly when 20 is divisible by $d$. The digits that divide 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5. So 21, 22, 24, 25 work: 4 numbers.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: Maria drew the following figures on square sheets of paper. How many of these figures have the same perimeter as the square sheet of paper itself?

solutions.title: Corners vs. notches
solutions.body:
Cutting a rectangle out of a **corner** of a square doesn't change the perimeter: the two new edges are exactly as long as the two missing pieces of the square's edges.

Cutting a notch out of the **middle of a side** adds extra length (the two sides of the notch).

- L: one corner cut → same ✓
- H: notches at top and bottom → longer ✗
- U: notch at top → longer ✗
- 4th figure: two corners cut → same ✓
- T: two corners cut → same ✓
- +: four corners cut → same ✓

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Push the edges out
solutions.body:
Imagine pushing every edge of the grey shape outwards to the edges of the sheet. For the L, the 4th shape, the T and the +, the edges slide right onto the square, so the perimeter is the same.

For the H and U, the inner vertical edges of the white notches can't be pushed onto the square's outline — they are extra length.

So 4 figures.

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: Patricia drives one afternoon at a constant speed to her friend. She looks at her watch as she leaves and when she arrives, as shown. In which position will the minute hand be when she has completed one third of her journey?

solutions.title: Find the travel time
solutions.body:
- When she leaves, the watch shows 12:30 (minute hand at 6, hour hand between 12 and 1).
- When she arrives, it shows 2:30 (minute hand at 6, hour hand between 2 and 3).

The trip takes 2 hours = 120 minutes. One third: $120 \div 3 = 40$ minutes. $12:30 + 40$ min $= 1:10$, so the minute hand points at the **2**.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Turn the minute hand
solutions.body:
In 2 hours the minute hand goes around twice. A third of that is $\frac{2}{3}$ of a full turn, which is 40 minutes on the dial.

Starting at the 6 (30 minutes), add 40 minutes: 30 + 40 = 70, which is 10 past the hour — the hand points at 2, as in (D).

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Johann stacks 1×1 cubes on the squares of a 4×4 grid. The diagram shows how many cubes were piled on top of each other on each square of the grid (HINTEN means *back*, VORNE means *front*). What will Johann see if he looks at the tower from behind?

solutions.title: Tallest stack in each column
solutions.body:
From the back you see, in each column, only the tallest stack.

Columns from left to right (in the diagram): $\max(4,3,2,1) = 4$, $\max(2,3,1,2) = 3$, $\max(3,1,3,1) = 3$, $\max(2,2,1,2) = 2$.

Looking from behind, left and right are swapped: 2, 3, 3, 4. That is picture (C).

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Rule out pictures
solutions.body:
The tallest stack is 4 (back-left corner), so the view must contain a column of height 4 — that rules out (A) and (D). From behind, the back-left corner is on Johann's **right**, so the tall column is at the right end: (B) or (C). Next to it is a column of height 3 (the second column has a 3), so it's (C), with heights 2, 3, 3, 4.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: 36 children voted for five students from their class. Each child was only allowed to vote once. The winner received 12 votes, and the student placed last received just 4 votes. If each student received a different number of votes, how many votes did the second-placed student receive?

solutions.title: Share out the middle votes
solutions.body:
The other three students got $36 - 12 - 4 = 20$ votes, all different, each between 5 and 11.

Possible sets (2nd, 3rd, 4th): $9 + 6 + 5$ and $8 + 7 + 5$. With 4th place at 6 or more, the three would need at least $8 + 7 + 6 = 21 > 20$.

So second place got 8 or 9 votes.

**Answer: (B) 8 or 9**

solutions.title: Test the choices
solutions.body:
- 10 votes for 2nd: the 3rd and 4th share 10, both at least 5 and different — impossible (5 + 5).
- 9: $9 + 6 + 5 = 20$ ✓
- 8: $8 + 7 + 5 = 20$ ✓
- 7 or less: at most $7 + 6 + 5 = 18$ ✗

So it's 8 or 9.

**Answer: (B) 8 or 9**

prompt: A 1×1×1 cube is cut out of each corner of a 3×3×3 cube. The picture shows the result after the first cube is cut out. How many faces will the final shape have?

solutions.title: Count old and new faces
solutions.body:
- The 6 big faces are still there (each just loses its corners, but stays one flat face).
- Each removed corner cube leaves a hole with 3 new small faces. 8 corners: $8 \times 3 = 24$.

Total: $6 + 24 = 30$.

**Answer: (D) 30**

solutions.title: Look at the picture
solutions.body:
After one cut, count the faces in the picture: 6 big faces + 3 small faces in the hole = 9 = $6 + 3$. Every further corner adds 3 more: $6 + 3 \times 8 = 30$.

**Answer: (D) 30**

prompt: How many different subtractions between two two-digit numbers are there which have the answer 50?

solutions.title: Count the smaller number
solutions.body:
We need $a - b = 50$ with $a$ and $b$ both two-digit numbers.

- $b$ is at least 10.
- $a = b + 50$ is at most 99, so $b$ is at most 49.

$b$ can be 10, 11, …, 49: that is $49 - 10 + 1 = 40$ choices.

**Answer: (A) 40**

solutions.title: List the ends
solutions.body:
Smallest: $60 - 10$. Largest: $99 - 49$. The first number goes from 60 to 99, which is $99 - 60 + 1 = 40$ subtractions.

**Answer: (A) 40**

prompt: In the last game of the hockey season there were lots of goals. In the first half 6 goals were scored and the visiting team was leading. After the home team scored another three goals in the second half, they won the match. How many goals did the home team score in total?

solutions.title: Try the first-half scores
solutions.body:
First half, 6 goals with the visitors ahead: home–visitors could be 0–6, 1–5 or 2–4.

Add 3 home goals: 3–6 (lose), 4–5 (lose), **5–4 (win)** ✓.

So the home team scored 5 goals.

**Answer: (C) 5**

solutions.title: Think about the lead
solutions.body:
Two scores that add up to 6 differ by an even number, so the visitors led by 2, 4 or 6. Three home goals only turn a lead of 2 into a win (a lead of 4 would at best become a loss by 1). So it was 2–4 at half time, and the home team finished with $2 + 3 = 5$.

**Answer: (C) 5**

prompt: Which of the figures below will cover the most dots when laid on the square shown? (Each ring of a figure sits on one square of the grid.)

solutions.title: Use the chessboard pattern
solutions.body:
The dots sit on every other square, like the black squares of a chessboard. So:

- a straight link (sideways or up/down) always joins a dot square to an empty square;
- a **diagonal** link joins two squares of the same kind.

Split each figure's rings into two teams this way; at most one team can be on dots. The bigger team has: (A) 4, (B) 4, (C) **5**, (D) 4, (E) 3 rings.

(C) is the only figure that can cover 5 dots.

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Place figure (C)
solutions.body:
Number rows 1–4 from the top and columns 1–4 from the left; the dots are where row + column is even.

Put the centre ring of (C) on row 3, column 3. Its three diagonal arms land on row 2 column 2, row 2 column 4 and row 4 column 4 — all dots. The bottom-left ring lands on row 3, column 1 — also a dot. Only the top-left corner ring misses.

That's 5 dots, more than any other figure can manage.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Matthias is catching fish. If he had caught three times as many fish as he has actually caught, he would have 12 more fish. How many fish has he caught?

solutions.title: Think in groups
solutions.body:
Three times as many = his catch + 2 more catches. Those 2 extra catches are the 12 extra fish, so one catch is $12 \div 2 = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

solutions.title: Try the choices
solutions.body:
With 6 fish: three times as many is 18, and $18 - 6 = 12$ ✓. (With 5: $15 - 5 = 10$ ✗; with 7: $21 - 7 = 14$ ✗.)

**Answer: (B) 6**

prompt: Numbers are written in the 4×4 grid: any two numbers in neighbouring squares (squares that share an edge) should have a difference of 1. The number 3 is already given. The number 9 will be used somewhere in the grid. How many different numbers will have been used once the grid is filled in completely?

solutions.title: How far can you get?
solutions.body:
Each step to a neighbouring square changes the number by exactly 1. The farthest square from the 3 (the opposite corner) is only 6 steps away. To reach 9 we need to go up by 6, so 9 must be in the opposite corner and **every** step on the way goes up by 1.

That forces each square to be 3 + (number of steps from the corner): the numbers used are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 — that's **7** numbers.

**Answer: (D) 7**

solutions.title: Fill the grid
solutions.body:
The only way to fit 9 is:

| 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
| 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |

Neighbours differ by 1 ✓. Different numbers: 3 to 9, which is 7.

**Answer: (D) 7**

prompt: Two buttons with smiling faces and two buttons with sad faces are in a row as shown in the picture. When you press a button its face changes, and so do the faces of the neighbouring buttons. What is the minimum number of button presses needed so that only smiling faces can be seen?

solutions.title: Find a 3-press solution
solutions.body:
Number the buttons 1–4: sad, smile, sad, smile.

- Press 4: buttons 3 and 4 change → sad, smile, smile, sad.
- Press 3: buttons 2, 3, 4 change → sad, sad, sad, smile.
- Press 2: buttons 1, 2, 3 change → smile, smile, smile, smile ✓

Three presses work.

**Answer: (B) 3**

solutions.title: Why not fewer?
solutions.body:
Pressing a button twice undoes it, so each button is pressed 0 or 1 times, and the order doesn't matter.

- Button 4 must stay the same: it is changed by presses of 3 and 4, so either both or neither.
- Button 1 must change: exactly one of buttons 1, 2 is pressed.
- Button 2 must stay: buttons 1, 2, 3 pressed an even number of times → button 3 must be pressed. So button 4 is pressed too.
- Button 3 must change: 2, 3, 4 pressed an odd number of times → button 2 is pressed, so button 1 is not.

The only solution is pressing 2, 3 and 4: 3 presses.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: If you start with three numbers, the 'addition machine' produces three new ones by adding together each pair of two. For instance, from the numbers {3, 4, 6} the addition machine makes {7, 9, 10}. If you use the addition machine again, these numbers become {16, 17, 19}. We feed the three numbers {20, 1, 3} into the addition machine and let the machine calculate 2013 times. What is the biggest possible difference between two of the three resulting numbers?

solutions.title: Differences never change
solutions.body:
Take $a, b, c$. The machine makes $a + b$, $a + c$, $b + c$. Compare two of them: $(a + b) - (a + c) = b - c$. So the differences between the new numbers are the same as between the old numbers!

Check with the example: {3, 4, 6} has differences 1, 2, 3, and so do {7, 9, 10} and {16, 17, 19}.

For {20, 1, 3} the biggest difference is $20 - 1 = 19$, and it stays 19 forever.

**Answer: (D) 19**

prompt: From an old model train set there are only identical pieces of track to use. Matthias puts 8 such pieces in a circle (picture on the left). Martin begins his track with 2 pieces as shown in the picture on the right (bending in opposite directions). He also wants to build a closed track and use the smallest number of pieces possible. How many pieces will his track use?

solutions.title: Count the turning
solutions.body:
Each piece turns the track by $\frac{1}{8}$ of a full turn, either left or right. A closed loop must turn exactly one full turn overall, so (left pieces) − (right pieces) = 8.

Martin already has a right-bending piece, so with 1 right piece he'd need 9 left: 10 pieces. But an S-bend (one left + one right) shifts the track sideways, like a step. To get back to the start, that sideways step must be cancelled by another S-bend on the opposite side of the loop. So he needs 2 right pieces and 10 left pieces: $12$ pieces.

**Answer: (B) 12**

solutions.title: Build it
solutions.body:
Start with Matthias's circle of 8 left-bending pieces. Cut the circle open at two opposite points and insert 2 extra pieces in each gap so the track turns right and then left again (an S-wiggle). Opposite wiggles shift the track by the same amount in opposite directions, so the ends still meet.

Pieces: $8 + 2 + 2 = 12$. With only one wiggle (10 pieces) the shift is not cancelled and the ends don't meet.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: 2013 people live on an island. Some of these people are truthtellers and the others are liars. The truthtellers always tell the truth, whereas the liars always lie. Each day one of the people says: 'When I have left the island, the number of truthtellers will be the same as the number of liars.' Then he leaves the island. After 2013 days there is no longer anybody living on the island. How many liars were living there to begin with?

choices.text: It is not possible to answer.

solutions.title: Work backwards from the last person
solutions.body:
- The last person: after he leaves, 0 truthtellers and 0 liars — equal, so he told the truth. **Truthteller.**
- The second-to-last: after he leaves, only 1 person (a truthteller) is left — not equal, so he lied. **Liar.**
- The third-to-last: after he leaves, 1 truthteller and 1 liar — equal: **truthteller.**

The pattern alternates: T, L, T, L, … counting from the last person. With 2013 people (odd), the truthtellers are the 1st, 3rd, …, 2013th from the end: 1007 of them. Liars: $2013 - 1007 = 1006$.

**Answer: (B) 1006**

solutions.title: Even or odd
solutions.body:
A statement 'the rest will be half truthtellers, half liars' can only be true if the number of people left behind is even. On day 1, 2012 people are left (even), on day 2, 2011 (odd), and so on. The people who leave an even number behind are on days 1, 3, 5, …, 2013 — 1007 truthtellers. Those who leave an odd number behind (days 2, 4, …, 2012) must be liars: 1006.

**Answer: (B) 1006**

prompt: 40 boys and 28 girls hold hands in a big circle. Exactly 18 boys give their right hand to a girl. How many boys give their left hand to a girl?

solutions.title: Groups of boys
solutions.body:
Around the circle the boys stand in groups (blocks of boys next to each other), separated by girls.

In each group, exactly one boy (at one end) gives his right hand to a girl, and exactly one boy (at the other end) gives his left hand to a girl. (If a group is a single boy, he does both.)

18 boys give their right hand to a girl → there are 18 groups → 18 boys give their left hand to a girl.

**Answer: (A) 18**

solutions.title: Count changes around the circle
solutions.body:
Walk around the circle clockwise. Every time you go from a boy to a girl, there must later be a change back from a girl to a boy, because you return to where you started. So the number of boy→girl changes equals the number of girl→boy changes. One counts boys holding a girl with their right hand, the other boys holding a girl with their left hand. Both are 18.

**Answer: (A) 18**
